# DBMS UNIT - I: Advanced Flashcards Deck (10 Cards)

### Q1
How do the Storage Manager and Query Processor coordinate during query execution and ACID transaction logging?

### Ans
The Query Processor parses declarative SQL, compiles it into an abstract syntax tree, evaluates heuristic equivalence rewrites (such as selection pushdown), and uses catalog statistics to determine the optimal physical execution plan. During runtime execution, physical operators (IndexScan, HashJoin) request disk pages from the Storage Manager. The Storage Manager's Buffer Pool Manager fetches pages into RAM frames using clock/LRU replacement, the Lock Manager enforces Strict 2PL/MVCC concurrency isolation, and the Recovery Manager logs modifications using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) to guarantee Atomicity and Durability.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *The Query Processor compiles declarative SQL into an optimal physical plan; the Storage Manager manages RAM frames, locks, and WAL logs.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  QP["Query Processor (Parser -> Optimizer -> Evaluation Engine)"] -->|Requests Pages| SM["Storage Manager (Buffer Pool -> Lock Mgr -> WAL Log Mgr)"]
  SM --> Disk["Physical Disk Blocks (Slotted Pages & Logs)"]
```

### Q2
How do Three-Tier enterprise web architectures achieve defense-in-depth security and connection scaling compared to Two-Tier?

### Ans
In Two-Tier Architecture, client workstations execute UI and application logic, establishing direct persistent socket connections (ODBC/JDBC) to the database; this exposes database network ports and exhausts database connection threads. In Three-Tier Architecture, clients execute presentation logic in public tiers (browsers/mobile apps), while business services run on load-balanced application server clusters in an intermediate subnet. The application servers maintain persistent, authenticated database connection pools, multiplexing thousands of client requests across worker threads. The database operates in a private, non-routable subnet, completely eliminating direct client exposure.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Three-tier architecture pools persistent database connections and isolates the storage engine behind application firewalls.*

```mermaid
graph LR
  Clients["Ephemeral Clients (Public Web)"] --> AppTier["App Servers (Connection Pools)"]
  AppTier --> DBTier["Database Cluster (Isolated Subnet)"]
```

### Q3
How do Disjointness (d vs o) and Completeness (Total vs Partial) constraints govern EER Specialization hierarchies?

### Ans
Specialization hierarchies enforce two orthogonal semantic constraints: (1) Disjointness Constraint: Disjoint (d) specifies that subclasses are mutually exclusive, so an entity instance can belong to at most one subclass. Overlapping (o) specifies that an entity may simultaneously belong to multiple subclasses. (2) Completeness Constraint: Total Specialization (double line) mandates that every superclass entity must belong to at least one subclass in the hierarchy. Partial Specialization (single line) allows a superclass entity to exist without belonging to any subclass. The four combinations (Disjoint-Total, Disjoint-Partial, Overlap-Total, Overlap-Partial) define exact subtype membership invariants.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Disjointness governs overlap (d = mutually exclusive, o = simultaneous); Completeness governs mandatory presence (Total = double line, Partial = single line).*

```mermaid
graph TD
  Super["Superclass"]
  Super -->|d / o| Circle((d or o))
  Circle --> Sub1["Subclass A"]
  Circle --> Sub2["Subclass B"]
  style Circle fill:#fff,stroke:#333
```

### Q4
What is Aggregation in the ER model, and why is it necessary to avoid redundant relationship modeling?

### Ans
Aggregation is an abstraction through which relationships are treated as higher-level entities. Classical ER modeling prohibits relationships from directly participating in other relationships. When a relationship must be associated with an external entity (e.g., an Interview relationship between Job_Candidate and Company must be associated with an Evaluation_Report), Aggregation encloses the relationship and participating entities into a composite rectangle, allowing external relationships to connect directly to it without converting the interaction into an ambiguous ternary relationship.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Aggregation elevates a relationship between entities into a composite higher-level entity that can participate in other relationships.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  subgraph Higher_Entity["Aggregated Entity"]
    E1["Employee"] --- R1["Works_On"] --- P1["Project"]
  end
  Higher_Entity --- R2["Monitored_By"] --- M["Manager"]
```

### Q5
How do ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, and RESTRICT enforce referential integrity during parent deletions?

### Ans
When a referenced primary key tuple in table P is deleted, the DBMS evaluates the declared foreign key referential action: (1) RESTRICT / NO ACTION: The deletion of the parent tuple is aborted immediately if any referencing child rows exist in table C; (2) CASCADE: The deletion automatically cascades, recursively deleting all child rows in table C whose foreign key matches the deleted primary key; (3) SET NULL: All referencing foreign key columns in child tuples in table C are automatically updated to NULL (requiring foreign key columns to be nullable); (4) SET DEFAULT: Referencing foreign key columns in child tuples are reset to their defined default value.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Referential cascades maintain integrity on parent mutations: RESTRICT aborts, CASCADE propagates deletions, SET NULL nullifies foreign keys.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  ParentDeleted["Parent Primary Key Deleted"] --> Policy{Foreign Key Rule}
  Policy -->|RESTRICT| Abort["Abort Transaction with Error"]
  Policy -->|CASCADE| DeleteChildren["Recursively Delete Child Tuples"]
  Policy -->|SET NULL| NullifyChildren["Update Child Foreign Keys to NULL"]
```

### Q6
How are Weak Entity Sets translated into relational schemas with composite primary keys and cascading foreign keys (Step 2)?

### Ans
In Step 2 of ER-to-relational mapping, for each weak entity type W with identifying strong owner entity E: create a relation R_W containing all simple and flattened composite attributes of W. Include as foreign key attributes in R_W the primary key attribute(s) of relation R_E referencing the owner. The primary key of R_W is the composite combination of the owner's primary key and the partial discriminator key of the weak entity set: PK = (PK_E, Discriminator). In SQL DDL, the foreign key constraint is declared with ON DELETE CASCADE to guarantee that child weak records are automatically pruned if the owner entity is deleted.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Weak entity table PK = Owner PK (as FK) + Partial Key, enforced in DDL with ON DELETE CASCADE.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  Owner["DEPARTMENT (Dept_No [PK])"]
  WeakEntity["DEPENDENT (Dep_Name [Partial], Age)"]
  Owner -->|Step 2| Rel["R_DEPENDENT (Dept_No [FK], Dep_Name, Age)"]
  Rel --> PK["Composite PK: (Dept_No, Dep_Name)"]
  Rel --> Cascade["ON DELETE CASCADE"]
```

### Q7
What are the four architectural options (8A, 8B, 8C, 8D) for mapping Specialization/Generalization hierarchies?

### Ans
Step 8 maps EER hierarchies via four strategies: (8A) Multiple Relations for Superclass and Subclasses: Create a table for the superclass and separate tables for each subclass sharing the same PK (foreign key to superclass); valid for any constraint. (8B) Multiple Relations for Subclasses Only: Create relations only for subclasses, replicating superclass attributes into each; valid ONLY for Total + Disjoint specializations. (8C) Single Relation with One Type Attribute: Merge entire hierarchy into one table with a discriminator column and nullable subclass attributes; valid ONLY for Disjoint specializations. (8D) Single Relation with Multiple Type Flags: Merge entire hierarchy into one table with individual Boolean flags for each subclass; optimal for Overlapping specializations.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *8A: normalized multi-table; 8B: leaf-only tables (total disjoint); 8C: single table with discriminator (disjoint); 8D: single table with flags (overlapping).*

```mermaid
graph TD
  Opt["EER Mapping Step 8 Options"] --> Opt8A["8A: Superclass + Subclass Relations (All Cases)"]
  Opt --> Opt8B["8B: Subclass Relations Only (Total Disjoint)"]
  Opt --> Opt8C["8C: Single Table + Type Code (Disjoint)"]
  Opt --> Opt8D["8D: Single Table + Boolean Flags (Overlapping)"]
```

### Q8
What are the Five Primitive Operators of Relational Algebra and the Closure Property?

### Ans
The five fundamental primitive operators of relational algebra from which all other query operations can be derived are: (1) Selection (sigma), (2) Projection (pi), (3) Union (U), (4) Set Difference (-), and (5) Cartesian Product (x). The Closure Property guarantees that the input operands of any relational algebra operator are relations, and the output result is ALWAYS a relation; this allows relational algebra expressions to be nested and composed into arbitrarily deep algebraic query trees evaluated by cost-based optimizers.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *The 5 primitive operators are sigma, pi, U, -, and x; Closure guarantees that every operation produces a valid relation, enabling operator nesting.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  Primitives["5 Primitive Operators"] --> S["1. Selection (sigma)"]
  Primitives --> P["2. Projection (pi)"]
  Primitives --> U["3. Union (U)"]
  Primitives --> D["4. Set Difference (-)"]
  Primitives --> C["5. Cartesian Product (x)"]
  Primitives --> Cl["Closure Property: Result is ALWAYS a relation"]
  style Cl fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#0288d1
```

### Q9
What are the performance, storage, and updatability trade-offs between Virtual Views and Materialized Views?

### Ans
A View is a virtual relation defined by an underlying query: (1) Virtual Views store only the SQL definition in the data catalog; upon query execution, the view is expanded inline into the base query (view inlining), guaranteeing real-time data freshness with zero redundant storage overhead, but recalculating joins on every request. (2) Materialized Views physically compute and persist result tuples on disk; they deliver lightning-fast analytical query performance for heavy aggregations, but incur storage overhead and require Periodic or Incremental View Maintenance (IVM) to stay synchronized with base table mutations. Under ISO SQL standards, a view is updatable only if it maps 1-to-1 to a single base table without aggregations, joins, or DISTINCT.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Virtual views store query text with zero storage and real-time freshness; Materialized views cache computed tuples on disk for high read performance.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  Def["CREATE VIEW Sales_Summary AS ..."]
  Def -->|Virtual View| Catalog["Stores SQL Definition Only -> Re-executed on Demand"]
  Def -->|Materialized View| DiskTable["Physically Persists Rows -> Requires Refresh Policies"]
```

### Q10
How do DDL statements execute within ACID transactional boundaries during Schema Evolution?

### Ans
In production relational database engines (e.g., PostgreSQL), Data Definition Language (DDL) statements execute within ACID transactional boundaries: (1) The DDL interpreter acquires schema locks (such as AccessExclusiveLock) on target tables; (2) System catalog tables (such as pg_class, pg_attribute, pg_constraint) are updated transactionally; (3) If a foreign key validation or type conversion check fails, the entire DDL transaction is rolled back via Write-Ahead Log undo passes, preventing corrupted catalog states; (4) Online schema evolution techniques allow fast-path column additions and concurrent index building (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) without locking table reads or writes.

💡 **Key Takeaway:** *Transactional DDL guarantees that schema changes (ALTER TABLE, DROP CASCADE) execute atomically under catalog transaction locks.*

```mermaid
graph TD
  DDL["ALTER TABLE Command"] --> Lock["Acquire Schema Lock on Table"]
  Lock --> Cat["Update System Catalog (pg_attribute)"]
  Cat --> Check{Constraint Check Pass?}
  Check -->|YES| Commit["Commit Catalog Transaction"]
  Check -->|NO| Rollback["Rollback via WAL Undo Passes"]
```
